passage:
Joining the school kabaddi team in Chennai changed Lakshmi's whole year. Practice at six gave her mornings a shape, the girls on the team saved her a seat at lunch, and somehow maths felt less frightening after an hour of sprint drills. She laughed more. She slept better.
Then the inter-school finals came near. The coach began shouting "no excuses" and timing everyone's sprints in front of the others. Vandana, the captain, told Lakshmi she should "look more like an athlete" for the team photo. Lakshmi began skipping lunch and lying awake replaying lost points.
One evening she sat on the empty ground, knees up, remembering how practice used to feel. The next day she told Vandana, "I play because I love it. I'm not changing my body for a photo." Then she asked the PE teacher to talk to the team about the pressure.

qa.q: What time was practice?
qa.a: Practice was at six.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel before the finals pressure began?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt happier and calmer; she laughed more, slept better and found maths less frightening.

qa.q: What steps did Lakshmi take when the sport became stressful?
qa.a: Lakshmi told Vandana she would not change her body for a photo and asked the PE teacher to talk to the team about the pressure.

qa.q: How might Vandana see the comment about looking like an athlete?
qa.a: Vandana may have thought it was only about the team's image, not realising it could push Lakshmi to skip meals and worry.

grounding: A teenager gains energy, structure and friends from a team sport, then grows stressed as pressure to win and to look a certain way takes over.

passage:
"You're smiling. You never smile in March," Ayesha said, unlacing her boots on the football ground.
"I know! Boards are in three weeks and I'm... fine?" Preeti laughed. "I think it's practice. After running, my brain's quieter. And I like having you lot."
"Same. Last year I ate lunch alone. Now I've got eleven people who'd fight for me."
Preeti's smile faded. "But Coach wants us to win districts. He keeps saying the forwards should be leaner. Rehana cried in the changing room."
"I heard."
"I don't want this to turn into another thing I'm scared of."
"Then let's say it. Together. To Coach, and to Ma'am if he won't listen. We play for this feeling, not a scoreboard."
Preeti nodded. "Together."

qa.q: When are Preeti's boards?
qa.a: Preeti's boards are in three weeks.

qa.q: What is Preeti worried about as the smile fades?
qa.a: Preeti is worried that football, which brings calm, will turn into one more frightening thing because of the pressure.

qa.q: What plan did Ayesha suggest?
qa.a: Speaking up together to Coach, and to Ma'am if he won't listen, so the team plays for the feeling rather than a scoreboard.

qa.q: What has the team changed for Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha went from eating lunch alone to having eleven people who would fight for her.

grounding: Teens draw calm and belonging from a team sport, and worry as pressure to win and to look leaner starts turning it into stress.

passage: The state kabaddi trials were on Sunday, and the heat in Madurai had closed the school ground all week. Keerthana's team practised at six in the morning on the temple lawn instead, with the coach, Hrithik Sir, shouting timings. She loved these girls. Since joining the team in Class 9, she'd stopped dreading school; the laughter, the bruises, the early-morning chai had given her days a shape. But this week felt different. Hrithik Sir kept saying, 'Lose on Sunday and forget the state team.' One of the seniors said Keerthana looked too soft to be selected. At night her mind raced. On Friday, after practice, her friend Anu found her crying behind the lawn. 'I used to love this,' Keerthana said. 'Now it's just more pressure.' Anu sat beside her. 'Then let's remember why we started. Chai first.'

qa.q: Where did the team practise that week?
qa.a: On the temple lawn.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling behind the lawn on Friday?
qa.a: She was stressed and sad, feeling that the sport she loved had become just more pressure.

qa.q: What small step did Anu suggest?
qa.a: Sitting together over chai and remembering why they started playing.

qa.q: How might Hrithik Sir's words affect the other girls?
qa.a: They might also feel anxious and pushed, turning practice into worry instead of fun.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose team sport gives her friends, structure and calm, until pressure to win and comments about her looks turn it into stress.

passage: Evening basketball in the Hyderabad colony court had become the best part of Irfan's day. Since he'd joined the older boys in Class 10, he'd stopped spending evenings alone on his phone, and exam worry felt smaller after two hours of running. He had friends who saved him a spot. Then one of them started joking about his thin arms. 'Stick boy.' The others laughed. Irfan began doing push-ups late at night in his room, and checking his arms in the mirror before every game. Basketball stopped being fun. His elder sister Pooja found him doing push-ups at midnight. 'You're exhausted, Irfan. Why?' He told her. Pooja sat on the bed. 'You loved that court because of the game and your friends, not your arms. Want me to come watch tomorrow?'

qa.q: What did one friend call Irfan?
qa.a: Stick boy.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after the jokes about his arms?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and anxious about his body, and basketball stopped being fun.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that could help Irfan?
qa.a: She asked gently, listened and reminded him why he loved the court, offering to come and watch.

qa.q: How might the friend who joked see the push-ups if Irfan told him?
qa.a: He might be surprised and sorry, not realising a joke had caused so much worry.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose sport gives him energy, friends and calm about school, until pressure to look a certain way turns it into stress.

passage:
'Good swim today, Chandrika.'
'Thanks, Imran. It was, actually. I felt light.'
'You always look happier after training.'
'I am. Before I joined the club, I was so tense about school. Now I have you lot, and Tuesday pizza, and I actually sleep.'
'So why did you look like you'd seen a ghost when your dad came in?'
Chandrika pulled her towel tighter. 'He's already talking about the national meet. He wrote my times on the fridge. If I don't drop a second by March, he says I'm wasting his time.'
'That sounds like a lot.'
'Some days I love it. Some days the water feels like an exam hall.'
Imran nodded. 'Maybe tell Coach? She's good at talking to parents.'
'Maybe.' She smiled faintly. 'Pizza first.'

qa.q: What does Chandrika's father write on the fridge?
qa.a: Her times.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when her father came in?
qa.a: She was anxious and pressured, as if she had seen a ghost.

qa.q: What step did Imran suggest?
qa.a: Telling the coach, who is good at talking to parents.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's father see his pushing?
qa.a: He may believe he is helping her succeed, not seeing how it turns the water into an exam hall for her.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose sport gives her friends, energy and calm about school, while a parent's pressure to win makes it another source of stress.

passage: Joining the school kabaddi team in Class 9 was the best thing I did. I used to dread Mondays; now I'd come home from practice tired but calm, and sleep like a stone. The team became my people. Uma, our captain, waited for me at the gate every evening. Then in Class 10 we reached the district finals, and everything changed. The coach started weighing us every week and shouting about 'looking like athletes'. I began skipping lunch and lying awake before matches, sick with worry about losing. Uma noticed. 'Swati, this was supposed to be the fun part.' We told our PE teacher about the weighing, and she spoke to the coach that same day.

qa.q: Who waited for Swati at the gate every evening?
qa.a: Uma, the captain.

qa.q: How did Swati feel before matches in Class 10?
qa.a: Swati felt sick with worry about losing and pressured about looking a certain way, lying awake at night.

qa.q: What did Swati and Uma do about the weighing?
qa.a: They told their PE teacher, who spoke to the coach that same day.

qa.q: What might Uma have felt noticing Swati's change?
qa.a: Uma probably felt worried and protective, missing the fun they used to share.

grounding: A teenager gains energy, calm and friends from a team sport until pressure to win and to look a certain way turns it into stress.
